subtopic: CANADIAN SECURITY INTELLIGENCE SERVICE ACT AND SECURITY OFFENCES ACT CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak to the report itself and, if it is not bending the rules, to comment in passing on the response of the government to it.

February 26, 1991
Routine Proceedings
The Canadian Security Intelligence Service Act was adopted in 1984 by the House of Commons. It essentially established a new regime for security intelligence in Canada. It provided that instead of the RCMP being responsible for security intelligence, a new agency, the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, would be created.
The 1984 legislation contemplated that there would be a review by a committee of Parliament five years after the act had passed. That committee was established in the summer of 1989 and was chaired by the distinguished member for Lethbridge, if I have his constituency correct. That committee worked hard for a year to produce this report, which is called In Flux But Not in Crisis.
I want to say at the outset that the committee report was unanimous. All members of the committee-Conservatives, Liberals and New Democrat-approved the recommendations in this report. It was the product not just of a unanimous report but of very extensive work by the committee. We had an extremely good staff, the committee worked very well together, and I want to pay a special compliment to the chair of the committee, who worked hard to draw us together to try to reach some constructive recommendations.
As with any unanimous report, it represents to some extent a compromise of various points of view. But we were very proud of the work that we did and felt that, in making this report, we were making a constructive set of suggestions and recommendations that would be for the good of this country and the good of the governing of this country.
Security intelligence is a difficult area, because essentially what we say to the government in establishing a security intelligence service is that we give you, the government, special powers in the interests of preserving the security of this country. But we have also learned over the years that it is essential to place certain restraints, constraints and restrictions on the special powers given to the government, to ensure that the rights of our citizens are not violated by the government.
As we in the committee got into the report, we actually found that there were two concerns. The first concern was in the area of civil liberties. It was whether CSIS, in the course of its work, was interfering with the civil liberties of Canadians; and whether there were adequate
checks and balances to ensure that on those occasions when citizens or residents of this country felt that their rights were being challenged and perhaps violated by CSIS, that there were sufficient remedies that would enable those actions to not only be reviewed and looked at but, where an error was found, to be corrected.
So, that was the first issue, civil liberties.
The second issue was whether CSIS and the government, in running this operation, was spending the public's money wisely.
By this current fiscal year, $190 million a year will be spent by CSIS. It has over 2,000 employees. What are those employees doing? What are they spending the money on? That leads to the question of why the secrecy, because we found the more we looked at it that the operation of CSIS was completely shrouded in secrecy and mystery.
Was the secrecy justified in the interests of protecting the country's security, was it covering up a government attack on the rights of citizens, or was it hiding a profligate waste of money on the part of this government agency? We found that CSIS was not going to tell us any of this. We found that the government was not going to give us any information on this. Now we find, when the government responds to the recommendation, that it has no intention of telling Parliament or the Canadian people what it is doing in Parliament's name and in the name of the Canadian people. We find that the government continues to hide behind the rubric of security and produces no justification for so doing.
Let me take a minute or two in summarizing some of the specific recommendations. The most important recommendation in my view is the recommendation that instead of a periodic review by Parliament there should be established a permanent subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General of the House responsible for security intelligence matters. The subcommittee would have a permanent security-cleared staff, have secure premises for its own work and would be able to receive information from the government in camera.
The subcommittee's role would be to focus on the question of estimates, is the government's and Parliament's and the people's money being spent wisely? It
February 26, 1991

would also focus on broad policy issues related to the interests of civil liberties and security in the country and the balance thereof. This particular recommendation owes its genesis to the McDonald commission which preceded the establishment of CSIS but was one in which all members of the committee concurred, one which makes good sense, one which is important if public confidence in CSIS is to be developed and maintained.
We found that the problem with a five-year review was that it took us some time as members of Parliament who were first coming to these issues to get up to speed. We found it took some time for the security agencies to develop some confidence in the committee and for us to develop a level of expertise necessary to ask the right questions of the right people. It seems to us that the system has matured to the point where a parliamentary subcommittee is important.
At one level the existing Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General has the mandate from Parliament to review the work of CSIS and other security agencies, including that of the RCMP. But that committee has a mandate to cover a range of topics and it was our view that it was important that a group of parliamentarians, per force a small group of parliamentarians, develop the kind of expertise which we in the committee felt we had gained in the year's work on the committee. That recommendation has been trashed and rejected by the government. The wisdom of all members, not just NDP members, but all members of Parliament, has been rejected by the government and instead the government wants to go back to the five-year review.

speechtext: Seven.

subtopic: CANADIAN SECURITY INTELLIGENCE SERVICE ACT AND SECURITY OFFENCES ACT CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Has it gone to seven? Seven-year review.
I have not even had a chance in the last 24 hours to read in detail all of the comments of the government. I read through it very quickly. I have some responsibilities now in another area.
A seven-year review.
One of the problems that the security people, the CSIS people, indicated to us was that there is sort of a lurching of response within the security intelligence
Routine Proceedings
community to the effect of imposing this special parliamentary review. There is no opportunity to get used to the fact of parliamentary review and, instead, what happens is they have to turn the House completely upside down trying to respond to the various questions and concerns that are exhibited by the committee.
When we went down to Washington and met with the CIA and other government people, we discovered that the senators and the congressional people in the States had found that they were able to develop over a period of time a level of confidence on both sides.
Let me say first, then, that I am extremely disappointed that the Solicitor General and the government have rejected this recommendation. I do not propose that it should be lost entirely, because in the final analysis it is within the jurisdiction of the Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General to make a decision as to how it is going to order its work. I would hope that all members of that committee will review this particular recommendation and see if they cannot bring themselves to accept the wisdom of this unanimous recommendation.
A second important recommendation was to broaden the review and oversight capacities to include other agencies than CSIS. What perhaps many members of the Canadian public and even members of Parliament may not appreciate is that the mandate of CSIS is confined to a particular area. The RCMP is also involved in security intelligence work; the Department of National Defence is involved in security work, and other departments have various agencies and various components of their work involved here.
Those agencies do not have the special power of CSIS, but it seemed to us to make sense that where there are concerns, including the secret spending of money for example, the communications security establishment's spending is not reviewed by Parliament. For practical purposes the RCMP's expenditures in this area are not reviewed by Parliament. DND's other expenditures are not reviewed by Parliament, and perhaps for good reason. It may well be that by revealing the details of those expenditures, exactly the wrong people get the information.

Routine Proceedings
Again we saw the importance of giving this parliamentary subcommittee, which could meet in camera and could receive security information, the responsibility for reviewing these other expenditures and the work done by other departments. As well we thought it important that the Security Intelligence Review Committee be given that mandate. Again that recommendation has been rejected.
One of the constraints on CSIS is the definition section of the legislation which limits but by its effect CSIS's mandates to the specially defined threats to the security of Canada.
One of the most important recommendations was the proposal to delete section 2(d) of that act which gives the government, through CSIS, the authority to use its special powers to look into what is called subversion under the act.
The more we looked at this section, the more we asked people who came before the committee: "What kind of subversion? What kind of activities are you talking about when you mean subversion?" We all agreed that CSIS needs to worry about terrorism. CSIS needs to worry about espionage. We as a Parliament are doing our responsibilities correctly when we give to this agency the duty to look into terrorism and espionage.
The more we looked at it, the more we found ourselves saying: "For the life of us, we can't see what kind of subversion we are talking about here." Subversion becomes very close, in some people's minds, to what, in another way of looking at it, would be perfectly legitimate political activities.
What we really are saying here, when the report recommended the deletion of 2(d), is that when challenges to the state get to the point of the use of violence or the threatened use of violence that is terrorism, and we say look into that.
When foreign governments spy in this country, we should know that that is happening. The history of this country suggests we should become very concerned when the government has its own definition of subversion and gives to itself the licence to look into groups that may have some difference of opinion with the government line of the day.
The most revealing testimony was from a former public servant, John Stams, who was vigorously defending the continued inclusion of clause 2(d) in the legislation. When he was asked by one of the members of the committee to give an example of subversion, his suggestion was those who would favour separatism or independence for Quebec.
I suspect it was that answer which provoked the government members, as well as the opposition members, to see how there could be an abuse of the rights of CSIS and the rights of government as embodied in the legislation.
No matter how many of us, as do virtually all members of Parliament, disagree with the proposition that Quebec or any other part of Canada should separate, we are in a democracy. Those people are entitled to that view as long as they express it within the democratic parliamentary system. That is the way in which we should work out these ideas. We should not give to our government the right to spy on those who are working within the democratic system on an idea, albeit one with which we disagree.
If people who have that view begin to contemplate violence in the pursuit of that political aim, then that becomes something which we should look into. Therefore, the unanimous view of the committee rejected by the government was that this section should be deleted.
There are many other important recommendations in this committee report. There are suggestions about the appointment to the Security Intelligence Review Committee which is Parliament's alleged watch-dog in this area.
We have seen the fiasco of the last appointment. The committee unanimously came up with ways which we believe would avoid that and restore to SIRC the confidence that it is entitled to.
We have various recommendations with respect to CSIS employees. I note with some disappointment that even though the director of CSIS said he favoured collective bargaining for CSIS employees, the government has merely said that it generally has no objection to that. What we do not see is a commitment by the government to amend the legislation to ensure that that right is available to the members.
There are a number of recommendations to improve the warrant process and to improve the rights of those who have been rejected for security clearances. Much of what happens in the security area comes under the general heading: "Security Review" and gives security clearances to people who are seeking to become citizens
February 26, 1991

of the country, who are seeking to immigrate into Canada, and who are seeking jobs in the public sector.
Yet, that system is not only bogged down with an enormous amount of paperwork. Not only were we not able to really get to the heart of how the system was working but, further, the checks and balances against an abuse of that system have not been addressed by the government report.
In sum, the answer of the government to this very comprehensive and well thought through report by the special committee reveals perhaps why this government has been in office simply too long.
It is hard for me to imagine that the government elected in 1984, after the previous 25 years in opposition, would so quickly jump to the defence of the security establishment and the bureaucrats and would fail its duty to this Parliament to respond with a greater open mind to the recommendations of this committee.
The rights of Canadians ought to be the prime concern of this Parliament. This motion I have on the floor now calls for concurrence in this report. In effect, it will represent a direction by this Parliament to the government that this report should be enacted.
We now have a contrast. We have the report of the parliamentary committee and we have the report of the government. They stand in contrast. It is important, in our view, that this House stand behind the committee, endorse the recommendations of the committee, and enact this charter for the next five years for the security intelligence system in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate my colleague from Victoria on a very excellent address this morning on the Solicitor General's answer to the special committee looking into the affairs of CSIS. I have a couple of questions I want to put to my hon. friend.
The first one comes from a passage at page 76 in the Solicitor General's response, which is entitled "On Course". The last paragraph on that page begins: "The government recognizes the need for consultation with opposition leaders regarding appointments to SIRC".
Routine Proceedings
If memory serves, there was a tremendous verbal blow-up, to put it mildly, when the present chairman of SIRC was appointed a year and a half or two years ago. At that time the former leader of this party made it very clear that he had not, in fact, been consulted, although there was provision at that time for consultation. There was simply a phone call. He was away from his office. The appointment went ahead and then he was apprised of the appointment following it.
My first question to the hon. member for Victoria is: Does this insertion in this Solicitor General's response on page 76 lend any greater credibility to the process than was already there and as it was used or abused some two years ago?
My second question relates to a statement the member made with respect to the special committee's journey to Washington where it consulted with officials on the government side. That is the CIA and other federal U.S. agencies in the security field.
I want to put this question to him. Did he get any impression at all that members of the CIA or any other related groups, such as the National Security Council, had suffered professionally or had their work been infringed upon in any way by the fact that in the United States of America, both at the Senate level and at the House of Representatives level, there are what we would call parliamentary or congressional oversight committees on an ongoing basis that look into the operation and management of those secret organizations?

subtopic: CANADIAN SECURITY INTELLIGENCE SERVICE ACT AND SECURITY OFFENCES ACT CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my friend for his question. I may say that as my duties changed, so did his. The member for Brant is now responsible within our caucus for matters of security intelligence. I would hope that if this subcommittee can in fact be established, he will have an opportunity to serve on it. I know he will serve with distinction in that event.
He asks two questions. First, with respect to the appointment of the Security Intelligence Review Committee, I could take the time to go through the whole sorry history of the last appointment. Instead, let me take my time to refer specifically to recommendation 80 of the committee's report. I will precede it by the comments of the committee.

February 26, 1991
Routine Proceedings
To appoint members to SIRC, the Prime Minister must first consult with the Leader of the Official Opposition and the leader of every party having at least twelve members in the House of Commons. The committee is aware that the process by which the current chairman of SIRC was appointed, caused some public concern.
That is an understatement. It goes on to say that the committee must hold the confidence of all Canadians.
In the end the committee recommended that section 34 of the CSIS Act be amended to require the Prime Minister: one, to notify in writing the leaders of each of the parties with more than 12 seats in the House of Commons that an appointment to SIRC is to be made; two, to request the leaders of each party so notified to put forward a short list of names of persons they believe to be qualified to be a member of SIRC; and, three, to communicate and discuss with the party leaders in the House so as to be apprised of their views on who should be appointed.
This recommendation specifically tightens up the procedures which would ensure that the opposition leaders are in fact consulted in the appointment of this important committee. I may say finally that the government merely recognizes the need to consult and fails to make a specific commitment that there should be an amendment to the CSIS Act in that respect. That is a cop-out on the part of the government.
The second question is the statement about the CIA and other intelligence agencies in the United States. What we found was that members of the security intelligence community in the United States who had been veiy apprehensive about the establishment of permanent committees of Congress to oversee their activities found that in the end it was in fact entirely helpful. They believed they were doing a good job and they found that the committees ultimately concluded that most of the time they were doing a good job. The committee served as a safety valve to deal with those issues where there was the inevitable screw-up on somebody's part.
We believed that as best we could find out CSIS was doing a good job. There were some safety valves established in the regime of the 1984 act, including the Security Intelligence Review Committee, but in our view those safety valves could be improved, in fact CSIS would benefit as with the rest of the security intelligence community from having permanent parliamentary overview, and they had nothing to fear from having permanent parliamentary review. I must say I ask when I look at the government recommendation of the government rejecting our recommendation: What is it that the government has to hide? Why does it not want us to look at how it is spending the money? Why does it not want us to look at what security intelligence is doing in Canada?

speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: CANADIAN SECURITY INTELLIGENCE SERVICE ACT AND SECURITY OFFENCES ACT CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the member for Victoria for affording us the opportunity to respond to this committee's report, the committee that was chaired by the hon. member for Lethbridge.
I want to say at the outset that I lived through the experiences of World War II as a young man. I would hope the member for Victoria would understand that the ethnic group from which I draw my roots and which I enjoy "enjoyed" considerably scrutiny during World War II and considerable public scorn at the time simply because of our generic names. I recall very clearly what it was like to be of Germanic extraction during World War II and the automatic suspicion that this incurred during wartime. Therefore, I and members of my caucus have first-hand experience of what it is like to be under unwarranted scrutiny.
I just want to say as forthrightly and as kindly as I can that we really do not need lessons from the member for Victoria about concern for civil rights in our society. While he is visiting with his seat-mate there, I would point out to him that those of us who have experienced that kind of scrutiny welcome the establishment of this agency, as well as of SIRC, as well as parliamentary review. We think it is a way of ensuring the civil rights of Canadians that these institutions be developed and these methods of review be developed. I just want to underscore to the member for Victoria that we as a government do not take this issue lightly. On the one hand we are accountable and responsible for the security of all Canadians from threats, but we are also responsible for the civil rights and the security of the civil rights of all Canadians.
We have a dual responsibility and we mean to discharge both of those responsibilities with vigour.
I debate the motion "that this House concur in the report by the special committee for the review of the

Canadian Security Intelligence Service Act and the Security Offences Act entitled, In Flux but not in Crisis".
This legislation is important to how we, as a society, deal with threats to our security, while protecting our democratic rights and freedoms. In 1984, when Parliament was studying the proposed CSIS and security offences legislation, it decided that there should be a review of the provisions and the operation of these acts five years after their coming into force.
I would like to commend the members of the special committee, chaired by the hon. member for Lethbridge, for the work that they carried out. The committee has made many observations and recommendations that deserve careful study by the security intelligence system of government.
Within the 150 days provided for by Standing Order 109, the government has tabled in Parliament its considered response to the committee's recommendations. I note that the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Lethbridge, in a press conference following the tabling of the report observed that the "review revealed no crisis or improper activities within our security and intelligence community".
It is also interesting to note that at the same press conference the hon. member for Victoria, the sponsor of this motion, stated "CSIS gets good marks from us as a clear improvement on the past".
The world has seen dramatic changes in the past five years. The Berlin wall has fallen and the cold war is over, at least we presume it is over. What will rise from the ashes is yet undetermined. I recall seeing a press report at the time when the Federal Republic of Germany was celebrating the unification of the two Germanys and on the night before the final act of unification the Soviet secret police were still meeting with the East German secret police, urging them to carry on their secret police activities. So while we hope the cold war is over, it means that some of those activities still carry on and those old habits die hard. Security is still a primary concern for the Canadian people.
I note also that the Prime Minister recently said to the conference of Interpol here in Ottawa:
Where states were once preoccupied by war, they must now also
worry about other threats to their security. The drug dealer, the
terrorist, the environmental criminal, the money launderer, the
Routine Proceedings
technological spy, the syndicates of organized crime. We must be as
vigilant and vigorous in co-operating to meet those new challenges
to national security as we have been to meet the old.
For CSIS, their mandate includes two of these threats, the terrorist and the technological spy.
Despite these changes in the world, then, most people would agree on the need for a system to protect Canadians from threats to their security and the need for a security intelligence service. In the government's view there can be no doubt that Canada needs CSIS.
The special committee concluded there is a need for a security intelligence service like CSIS. I also note that the committee found no witnesses who took the position that security intelligence was no longer necessary or that the mandate of the civilian domestic security intelligence service should revert to the RCMP.
Threats to our security do exist. Consider the threat from terrorism. Canadian democracy depends upon a climate of freedom, where political objectives are pursued through open discussion, debate and lawful advocacy. This climate, as well as public safety, are jeopardized when any person or group seeks to gain their political objectives by carrying out acts of violence or by threatening to do so.
In the 1980s the threat of terrorism became an immediate security concern and this government has directed CSIS to treat terrorism as its first security intelligence priority. Our first line of defence must be intelligence.
The other major threat, espionage, has been an ongoing reality since the emergence of nation states. All nations seek to advance their position in the world. Some resort to covert means to do so, and this threat exists today despite changes in the international political climate. Despite these changes, the threat posted to the security of Canada by hostile intelligence services continues to be high.
Canada must have the means to protect itself from such threats, whether they take the form of traditional espionage or attempts to steal knowledge of sensitive high technology. The government owes it to Canadians who are devoting their careers to providing their country with scientific advances. The special committee also concluded that terrorism and espionage continue to threaten Canada and Canadians.

February 26, 1991
Routine Proceedings
When this parliamentary review began, the government stated it believed that the Canadian Security Intelligence Services Act and the Security Offences Act are sound pieces of legislation which are working as Parliament intended. The special committee has stated it is satisfied that the basic architecture of the act was sound, functioned well and should be preserved.
I would like to remind the House of some of the fundamental views the government took into the review process as outlined by the new Solicitor General when he appeared before the special committee.
The CSIS Act provides a statutory framework for balancing . effective national security with respect for individual rights and freedoms. The CSIS Act defines CSIS' mandate to collect intelligence and advise the government on threats to the security of Canada. It gives the service the powers necessary to fulfil that mandate.
The act that sets up a unique guidance system for the agency, consisting of a legislative framework that defines and limits the powers of CSIS, political control and accountability, a system of judicial controls and significant external review by the Security Intelligence Review Committee.
Finally, the act provides a mechanism for hearing the complaints of any person or group about any aspect of CSIS's activities.
The Security Offences Act confirms the security offences enforcement and protective security responsibility of the RCMP. These acts provide a well-conceived legislative framework that allows flexible response for changing circumstances, within an unprecedented legal and policy framework which is unmatched in the world.
The government has used policy direction to guide the interpretation and implementation of these acts. All of the key players in the security intelligence system in Canada have worked hard to ensure the legislation operates in a practical and effective manner.
The service has developed and operates on the basis of a sound and stringent targeting process. A rigorous process is in place for warrant applications, and the reporting function of the service is being enhanced to
improve and reflect better the process of policy development and decision-making within the government.
The Inspector General and the Security Intelligence Review Committee have carried out their roles in an orderly and rigorous way, and I think the member for Victoria would agree with that.
The reports of the Inspector General reassure the minister that CSIS is conforming to the law and ministerial policy directions while SIRC, by its annual reports, which the minister must table in Parliament, completes an annual cycle of public accountability for CSIS. To infer that another jurisdiction like the United States has a scrutiny that Canada does not have is a little bit misleading and I hope that the member for Victoria would agree with that.
Finally, the RCMP and CSIS have measures in place and a working relationship that ensures effective co-operation. This is how the legislation is working today.
As legislators, I think we can all appreciate that five years is not a long time to implement fundamental change. Nevertheless, a great deal has been accomplished. The CSIS Act and the Security Offences Act went through an initial working-in period. The new acts were a dynamic and self-correcting system which provided a sound security system for balancing effective national security with respect for rights and freedoms.
After three years of experience with the new CSIS Act, the need for accelerating the transition process became apparent in 1987 through internal warning signals and external reports of the SIRC and the Joint Parliamentary Committee on Official Languages. The government established an independent advisory team headed by the Hon. Gordon Osbaldeston to determine how CSIS should evolve more rapidly towards meeting the goals set forth by Parliament.
As you know, the Osbaldeston report, released in November 1987, concluded that the CSIS Act was basically sound and that CSIS is an important national institution staffed by dedicated professionals. However, after three years, the evolution of CSIS needed the discipline of an action plan to accelerate its transition to a modem security intelligence agency.
February 26, 1991

The government accepted the Osbaldeston report's recommendations as a mid-course correction for the service, and I hope the member acknowledges that.
I would now like to describe some of the major accomplishments achieved by the government since the act was proclaimed in 1984.
In the area of the internal management of CSIS:
1.	The director now plays a strong role in managing intelligence operations; for example, he personally chairs the key internal operational committees.
2.	CSIS has adopted a tighter and sharper operational policy on targeting.
3.	Deputy directors responsible for corporate management and for human resources and official languages have been appointed in order to improve CSIS's internal planning and accountability process, human resource development and official languages capacity.
4.	CSIS has been provided with an adequate budget, brought for the first time to a level commensurate with its requirements and CSIS personnel will be brought together in one headquarters building.
5.	CSIS's training academy has been re-established in Ottawa with a range of training programs in both official languages.
In the area of government control of CSIS, ministers have conveyed to CSIS, by formal direction, the following points: The government's national requirements for security intelligence to keep intelligence production in line with the needs of the government. The definition of threats to the security of Canada found in section 2 of the CSIS Act defines the parameters for collection of intelligence. These broad subject areas can be further refined to focus more directly on the intelligence needs of consumer departments. Consumer needs shall, in future, be organized under five national interest areas within which strategic information on threats to the security of Canada may be reported to the government.
This direction sets out five national interest areas: One, public safety; the ability of people to engage in ordinary social activity without fear of harm. Two, integrity of the democratic process; the functioning of those institutions, rights and freedoms fundamental to the political well-being of a democratic society. Three, security of government assets; the responsibility of the
Routine Proceedings
government to protect those human, intellectual and physical assets which it manages in trust for the Canadian people. Four, economic security; the conditions necessary to sustain a competitive international position, provide productive employment and contain inflation. Five, international peace and security; the ability of the international system to evolve while avoiding war, containing regional conflicts and minimizing violence.
The directive also specifies how ministers expect a director to be accountable. It gives direction of the general conduct of investigations which includes the principles enunciated by the McDonald commission. The investigative means must be proportionate to the gravity of the threat posed, and the probability of its occurrence. The need to use various investigative techniques must be weighed against possible damage to civil liberties and valuable social institutions.

Mr. Speaker, I thank you for recognizing me and I am pleased to have an opportunity to address in debate the motion by my colleague from Victoria.
Before I launch into the body of my remarks, I want to give some credit where credit is due. Credit is due to the relatively large number of individuals who work in the security intelligence establishment here. I am talking about the career men and women in CSIS, the RCMP, and those other agencies that, as far as we can see from our review, have operated and served well and are continuing to do so even in the current circumstances where a significant challenge has been presented to them.
That is not to say that mistakes have not been made. It is not to say that mistakes are not being made. One of the problems we have in this area is that if they are making mistakes, they are apparently not subject to the kind of scrutiny that other government officials would be in such circumstances.
Our committee, the special committee of this House, spent over a year working in this field. It was an intensive study. We operated within a framework that frankly caused a number of restrictions.
Ultimately, compromises were made that permitted us to achieve many, but not all, of our goals as a committee.
We encountered a learning curve. It took us a few weeks to realize that the area we were studying was an area none of us had truly had an opportunity to see previously. It took a while for us to realize that. Then we were able to proceed in our review of this relatively closed field of government activity.
The reason we were asked to do the review is contained in the original statute itself. This Parliament asked other parliamentarians to review this law after five years. This was not an ad hoc committee developed to

February 26, 1991
Routine Proceedings
review CSIS. It was planned well in advance by parliamentarians who knew and understood that the laws being developed in this area might well need some fine tuning.
The title of the government's response is On Course-National Security for the 90s. Well, national security is a combination of security intelligence and foreign intelligence. The title "National Security" is slightly pretentious because it appeared in our review that the whole field of foreign intelligence was kept pretty much away from CSIS, from the RCMP Security Offences Act, and resided for the most part with the the Department of External Affairs and the Interdepartmental Committee on Security and Intelligence within the Privy Council Office. So, we did not have a good look at national security.
One of the recommendations we made, to set up an office of national assessments, as other jurisdictions have done, was rejected by the government. We will not have that balanced, objective review of foreign intelligence and security intelligence that comprises a complete picture of national security.
We have already entered the age of technological big brother. I referred earlier today to the potential for electronic eavesdropping upon all Canadians. Well in-tentioned, I am sure, but electronic eavesdropping of the most intensive sort. A form of eavesdropping where anything that is said, anything that moves, whether it is audio or video, whether it is an electronic field, can be monitored through walls from distances of miles. I believe that the mechanisms Parliament has put in place, and I think all of the committee believes this, need fine-tuning, need updating. If the government thinks it is moving into the 1990s and ready for the 1990s in this field, it is my view it is doing it with a rear-view mirror. If the government had paid closer attention to the recommendations of the committee it would be much further ahead.
I would like to hope that after the next federal election, the next Government of Canada will be able to pay closer attention to this area.
I want to touch on five or six areas of recommendation that the government failed to deal with. The committee had hoped that the Solicitor General and the Director of CSIS would expand on the areas of ministerial direction. These directions are the framework operating documents that are prepared by the Director and put in place for CSIS as it carries out its work, both for work that involves interests of surveillance and work that is simply analysis.
We had hoped that those directions could be expanded. To give some credit to CSIS, since we made our report one of the more important areas of ministerial direction was created and put in place. That had to do with the definition of the threat mandate. There are many more areas where we had concern and there is still a lot of work to do.
In dealing with review mechanisms, I mentioned earlier that CSE does not even show up on the screen of review mechanisms. The parliamentary secretary said review is referred to in the government's response. Well, the four items referred to as scrutiny, or review, or monitoring are in-house legal counsel from the justice department.
That is not review. That is not supervision. That is not scrutiny. That is not monitoring. Every department in government has a Department of Justice counsel at the other end of the phone. That is a zero.
The second item is that CSE consults frequently with senior officials in the Privy Council Office, the Department of National Defence, and Department of External Affairs. They are the same people that they carry on their work with. That is not supervision, review, or monitoring.
The government says that CSE is subject to internal Department of National Defence administrative review, so is every other government department. The govem-ment also says that CSE submits strategic plan and policy proposals for review by the Interdepartmental Committee on Security and Intelligence; that is the Privy Council Office, the people they work with. That is a closed shop, and that is not supervision or review.
Let us not be misled that the government has replied effectively to that question. CSE is not monitored. It is not reviewed, and it is still operating out there without review.
We had a lot of time to look at the operations of the national security investigations directorate of the RCMP and it was our view that when problems or complaints arose with regard to the security work of the RCMP, those matters should be referred to the Security Intelligence Review Committee as a complaint, but that they
February 26, 1991

should be investigated by the RCMP special complaints commission.
That is not interference with the RCMP. That is simply a procedural consolidation of the complaints process. We thought it would be easier if the public felt there had been an error made and a complaint warranted if it could be made to one location, the Security Intelligence Review Committee.
We felt that the Security Intelligence Review Committee should be able to make special reports to Parliament. It is the organization that works for Parliament, for Canadians. It should be reporting to Parliament whenever it feels the need, whenever it is appropriate.
Instead the law now says that it reports annually. I do not think that is adequate, our committee did not think it was adequate. It should have the ability, the jurisdiction, to submit a report to Parliament for us, for our constituents, whenever it feels so advised.
Government did not accept that recommendation.
We felt in the complaint process that the Security Intelligence Review Committee ought to have the ability to self-initiate a complaint. The government did not agree with that, nor did it agree with our view that a complaint could be made directly to the Security Intelligence Review Committee.
Although I referred to that process earlier, in fact the law requires that all complaints go to the director of CSIS. In other words, go right to the agency that you are complaining about in the first place. We felt there should be a way for a complaint to go to the Security Intelligence Review Committee directly.
I want to talk about the actual parliamentary review. The member for Victoria referred to our study of the review mechanism used in the U.S. Congress and I thought I detected some scepticism from the other side about that study.
In the United States 25 years ago they were roughly where we are now; there was not an effective congressional review of security and intelligence matters. They had some problems 20 years ago, 15 years ago, at the time of the Vietnam war, and some other problems occurred . subsequent to that. Legislators there then began to act. The result now is that a standing committee of Congress,
Routine Proceedings
a joint committee on security and intelligence, reviews all matters and reviews the appropriations and budget matters for all security and intelligence agencies within the U.S. government.
That, one would expect, could cause a problem; but I am advised by officials, experienced officials including the former head of the Central Intelligence Agency who visited with us, that that process works very well, that there are no leaks, that the security and intelligence establishment actually appreciates the oversight that exists. They appreciate the fact that they know we are looking, the legislators are looking at what they are doing at all times, and that helps to keep them honest. Shedding sunshine on the process has been effective in the United States. That is what we are told.
In terms of a further review here as an alternative to a parliamentary subcommittee which we had suggested, the government replies: "We will take a look at the matter again in seven years", near the end of the 1990s. One way to get through the 1990s is to have a review at the end of it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate this morning. I do not intend to take my full 20 minutes, as I know there are two others who would like to make a contribution as well.
I do not wish to reiterate the very excellent arguments that my friend and colleague from Victoria presented at
the outset of the debate this morning in moving the concurrence motion. Rather, I would first of all like to speak in more general terms with respect to secret intelligence organizations, secret agencies and the secret world, itself, in a democracy, and the place and responsibility of those agencies in a democratic society.
I know that perhaps to some extent we are all captives or many of us are captives of current literature in the field and sometimes we are swept away by fiction as opposed to fact. But the facts still remain that most if not all countries, whether totalitarian or democratic, do have and indeed need secret intelligence services in order to keep them apprised of any threats or potential threats to the security and safety of the state. That goes without saying. We are not arguing, obviously, whether or not we should have a security and intelligence service. The crux of the matter surely is that service's place in our society, how it operates in our society and to whom it should be ultimately responsible.
I would argue this morning, in view of the Solicitor General's total rejection of the 117 recommendations of the special committee, that the ultimate authority for establishing CSIS was and still is the House of Commons and therefore CSIS is ultimately responsible to the House of Commons, its maker. That is theory but that is also practice. If we are to retain the basic precepts of democracy in a parliamentary system, all government agencies, whether it is the CSE or the intelligence networks of DND or the External Affairs Department or CSIS, or indeed SIRC, all must be ultimately responsible to Parliament.
How do we go about facilitating that relationship and that ability to be responsible to this Chamber? Obviously it would be cumbersome. It would be indeed impossible to force an agency such as CSIS to be responsible to the entire House, or to come before open committees of this House and present arguments or counter-arguments to questions put to it, or to justify its budget perhaps, or to justify its actions. But surely one way, a way in which our colleagues to the south of us in Washington have found an answer and have set up a system, is to have an oversight or a review committee of this House meeting, no doubt most of the time but not all the time in camera, and charged with the responsibility of maintaining confidences and having adequate research staff and advisers in order to facilitate its work. Then CSIS could be directly responsible to an appendage of this House or
February 26, 1991

part of this House, which would be that all-party committee.
That all-party committee would have horrendous responsibilities. There is no question about it. It would not be a normal type of committee, but it would be a vital link and it would keep alive that very important relationship in terms of accountability and responsibility.
A government agency-in this case CSIS-responsible to a minister, yes, but also responsible directly to the body that created it and that is responsible for it, namely, a special committee of this House of Commons.
American congressmen in the House of Representatives, and indeed the senators, have already gone ahead and established such review committees. The committees have not in any way infringed upon the operations or the operational integrity of such organizations as the CIA or the National Security Council and the various military intelligence organizations or intelligence gathering organizations in that country.
Yet, in his response, the Solicitor General when he tabled his report yesterday, thoroughly rejected the idea that we should set up a special subcommittee in this House for that very purpose.
I am very disappointed because of that lack of sensitivity on the part of a cabinet minister in a very sensitive area. Yet, on page 77 of that very report, On Course, subtitled National Security for the 1990s, the Solicitor General writes: "To refuse to discuss national security issues publicly with Canadians is to encourage mistrust and ignorance".
That is the problem we are faced with this morning. We have a minister who recognizes that to deny public access to the workings of his department, specifically CSIS, is to encourage mistrust. That is exactly what he says in his report. On the other hand, he denies the veiy access that we are seeking in this House, that is the special committee. I do not understand his logic or indeed his lack of logic.
I could speculate that the Solicitor General has become a captive of his officials, that his deputy and the director of CSIS have said: "No way',' and the minister has had no choice but to go along with his senior officials.
Routine Proceedings
He has agreed with them. If my speculation is correct, that is indeed regrettable, and I am putting it very mildly when I say so.
Experts on the subject of secret intelligence organizations generally agree that upwards of 80 to 90 per cent, if not more, of the work that those organizations carry on is in fact not secret. The reason they insist on retaining the wall of secrecy around them, they meaning the officials within those bodies, is simply self-promotion. It is survival.
If you remove the emperor's clothes, he is no longer an emperor. If you remove the secrecy or a lot of the secrecy, the aura of secrecy disappears and it becomes just another agency of the Crown. Therefore it is doubly difficult to get appropriations and the proper funding.
While I am on that subject, I should insert here that CSIS is one of the few government agencies that for the past five years since 1985-86 and on into 1990-91 has consistently increased its funding with an average of 14.4 per cent a year. No doubt, this afternoon when the budget comes down, we will not see any decrease in that apportionment of public funding.
Yet, when we stand in this place or in a committee where we should be asking questions about the financing and funding of CSIS, we are told that they cannot give us the answers unless we are in camera. Even then I doubt whether they would give us specific answers to specific funding questions because it is contrary to the act.
I was here in the early 1980s and it was not the intention of Parliament at that time to prevent us from finding out in general ways what the Solicitor General, the deputy solicitor general and the director of CSIS were all about not in terms of specific operations, but in terms of policy and funding.
For what purposes were Canadian tax dollars going and were they going appropriately, honestly and fairly toward the legal execution of the duties of CSIS itself? We cannot find that out. We have no way of knowing whether or not public funding is not only wisely spent in CSIS, but that it is effectively spent. Every time the director comes back with his proposed new budget, it is all worked out in secret and in private. We have no input, but worse than that we have no say. We cannot reduce

February 26, 1991
Routine Proceedings
the budget and we cannot even ask why the money is being spent and for what purpose.
I also want to refer to another aspect of this which has already been dealt with this morning, that is the choosing process of members of the review committee. I do not know any of these people personally, although I believe one is a former member of the House of Commons. I have never met Mr. Bassett. I do not know what his capabilities are. The record to date certainly raises eyebrows, but that is as far as I will go; I will leave it at that. The process of choosing Mr. Bassett was totally unacceptable and, as has already been stated, it was not a result of consultation. It was take it or leave it. Even at that, we were apprised of the appointment after it was made and had no way of effectively opposing it in any way.
To choose a person for such an important office, to chair the Security Intelligence Review Committee which is charged with veiy serious responsibilities, to allow that choice to be done in such a haphazard way and to go to a party hack-and there is no other way of putting it; Mr. Bassett may have many fine attributes as a gentleman and as a human being, but he is a strong, and always has been, partisan supporter of the party in power-this is not the kind of person that calls out for that kind of appointment. It should be somebody in my view above politics, somebody outside the political arena, somebody who has a gift for that kind of office. It is very important that the head or the chairman of SIRC be seen to be totally removed from the political scene, and that did not happen.
There are several other aspects of the special committee's report that I could expound upon this morning, but I realize that time is limited and that there are two other members of the House who wish to speak. I do, however, in closing also wish to comment very briefly on the committee's recommendation to delete section 2.(d) in the definitions section, specifically the definition of subversion.
In a democracy we not only tolerate, but indeed promote healthy, lawful descent and controversy. We should not be afraid of it. We should stand up and accept it, argue with it if one wishes or support it, depending on which side of the argument one happens to be at any one time. But that kind of activity has been in the past and
continues to be interpreted by some individuals as being, if not subversive, at least borderline. The physical approach that the police and CSIS and other organizations, the RCMP for example, take in terms of demonstrations and marches, no matter what the purpose is for, is such that they are all suspect. The cameras come out, pictures are taken and are put away in some folder or filing cabinet or put on microfiche or something, in case somewhere down the line they may wish to withdraw those pictures and say: Ha, ha, so-and-so was at that demonstration at that point in time. Therefore, now we really suspect that he or she may be a subversive individual depending on the circumstances.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to rise and say a few words with respect to the government's official response entitled On Course which members know is a response to the committee report entitled In Flux. It was a unanimous committee report to which the government has now responded.
I can understand the frustrations of members. Our document had over 100 recommendations and the gov-
February 26, 1991

emment has not come out with a chart responding exactly to every one of the recommendations that we have made. I want to say that I am still proud to have been a member of that committee. I believe that members of the opposition, who were mostly new members of Parliament, should be and can be immensely proud of the contribution they have made. I do not say that lightly because it needs to be seen in the context.
Many of us remember the pre-1980 regime that had gone on since the beginning of Confederation where the security issues were developed within the RCM Police. There was virtually no public accountability at all. Indeed, most members of Parliament did not even know what the CSE was, the Canadian Security Establishment, in the latter years. That was the way the system worked through all the many years before 1980.
As a result of events in Quebec and the McDonald commission, a new regime came forth and it became law in 1984. That regime really did provide a lot of accountability, primarily through an independent agency called SIRC, which has members of all three political parties. That was felt to be the primary mechanism to hold the civilian agency accountable.
We found in our group that in fact has worked very well. But again I really want to take members back to the point that the system has incrementally been getting better and better. There has been more and more information made available to members of Parliament, to the SIRC committee, which as I say, has representatives from all three political parties, and which does a tremendous job day after day. We members of Parliament become so busy and occupied with the many other pressures in our lives, we cannot put the time into that which we might like to and what the topic deserves. That is why our committee really felt that SIRC was an excellent agency and deserved to continue on.
With respect to the government's response, I think that the most important part of it is that for the first time we have a document that is available to every Canadian who wants to have it, with its major authoritative setting out of the whole area of security. Anybody who reads this document will know all of the players, they will know the mechanisms for control, accountability and responsibility. That in itself is very powerful information for people to have. As a result of my experience here in Ottawa, I
Routine Proceedings
am firmly of the view that if an agency or a government gets out of line, brown paper envelopes are very quickly leaked. Given the number of civil servants, the number of photocopy machines, one just cannot get very far out of line. Information gets out. As long as the opposition is vigilant and the standing committee on justice is vigilant, these things can be raised.
We have a vigilant media in Canada. Not only are they vigilant, but some members are very knowledgeable, indeed, experts in this area of security and intelligence. We have an ever-increasing body of researchers and academics who now have their own association called CASIS. They are very sophisticated, operated by fine women and men. So I believe it is impossible for the same mistakes that the RCMP made to occur again, that certainly on a broad basis information will get out.
Just that in itself, to my mind, makes the review that we conducted in 1990 worth it. But there are other advantages and I suppose the other most important was that the government has accepted the fact that there should be another review in 1998.
I know from the evidence we received from all the major players in the security intelligence field that they felt a parliamentary review was like the sword of Damocles over them. They really did have some fear and apprehension about coming before us because we do represent this whole Parliament. However, for the most part, I think our committees do very good work in that area.
The annual reports that the minister and the director have to give to Parliament directly is a major step forward. It lets the justice committee have another avenue to get the minister before the committee and ask specific questions. The last point I want to make is that it will really depend on us as members of Parliament. This Parliament has all sorts of committees. While I do not sit on the committee for disabled Canadians, handicapped Canadians, I trust that my colleagues on that committee are asking the right questions, are taking that area of our public life and advancing it step by step just as we who had the responsibility to do the security review. We were successful in getting more information out to the public. We have incrementally increased the knowledge that Canadians and our fellow members of Parliament have.

February 26, 1991
Routine Proceedings
To my mind that is the whole system. That is the way that democracy works. It is slow. It is tedious. We all sit for hundreds of hours on these committees and get absolutely no political credit back in our own riding in terms of votes. However, it does strengthen the public life of the nation and it does hold our bureaucrats more and more accountable. We all agree, including the bureaucrats, that accountability is the secret. It is a day by day, step by step building of the system.
I think the other major advantage of having gone through the process is that we have built the confidence level. It was most interesting when we started and the CSIS people were coming before us. You could see they were really nervous, perhaps to the point of being scared that the national security of the country would be somehow jeopardized by this committee. They do have an important role and we all recognize that we need to have security.
The world is not a playground. It is not an area where people are honest and straightforward. There is a lot of information that needs to be kept secret. We all recognize that. But they were somehow fearful that the whole system was going to collapse. The fact of the matter is the system has not collapsed. This is a result of very responsible conduct on the part of the members of the committee, both the government backbenchers and the opposition members.
As that process went on throughout the year we could just feel that they were prepared to share more and more information. We received some confidential briefings, the information from which has been held confidential and will always be held confidential because none of us is going to subvert our country just for the sake of a question in the House of Commons, or some narrow advantage to us personally, or our party. People do not work like that.
We found that was much more the case in the United States where, over a period of years, they had built confidence levels so that their elected congressmen had more information than we did.
It is true that the two systems are a bit different. A congressman in the United States system has more individual accountability back to the nation. They have an obligation, constitutionally, to make sure the government continues to operate. In our system, we are little different simply because the cabinet has to be chosen from this House and to be accountable to this House.
If the Prime Minister was elected separately and could choose the cabinet from all of the people in the country, that would be a different type of body. We would then be pure legislators and would have an obligation to make the system work; whereas here, there is not that same obligation. The opposition's objective is to point out all the defects of the government, but as well to try and bring the government down by way of a whole series of non-confidence motions.
If opposition members got secret information that could be damaging to the government, they would be in a very tough position and I think would almost have to reveal that information, because they have an obligation to bring the government down under these non-confidence motions.
That was what we debated. It is a troubling issue, and there is no easy solution.
I think we should move to a bit more of a congressional form of government, because I would like to be known as a legislator and I would like to be able to be held accountable by my own electors for how I stood on the issues. It would get away from a lot of this partisanship; we would then be working across party lines. There would be lots of times when I would be voting with the opposition, and vice versa.
I think that would be good for our countiy, but for other reasons.

Their cabinet ministers, when they become part of the executive council, take on a different constitutional role, take on a different hat and have very different responsibilities. They have sworn special oaths of secrecy. It is amazing how quickly it makes them much more responsible-and much quieter, if I can put it that way. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the limited amount of time left, I did want to make a few comments because I had the privilege of working on the committee. It was a good committee under the chairmanship of Mr. Thacker and it worked very well.
There were unanimous decisions on almost every point and it was a unanimous report. I think to a degree, what is a little upsetting in the final result is how the government has treated a hard-working committee's unbiased and unanimous recommendations. There were 117 recommendations and by my quick count I think the government responded to one and a half out of the 117.1 do not think that, quite frankly, is the proper approach.
The other interesting thing is we have matured in this country as far as CSIS is concerned. When the agency was first formed in 1983-1984, there was a large hue and cry about the land. That is not the case now, nor was it as
Routine Proceedings
the committee did its work. There were constructive suggestions from a number of individuals, but there was not the concern that existed in 1984. So with that in mind, I think the committee came up with the proper balance. The key element that came out of the report, which the government has chosen to ignore, is the one dealing with oversight.
Mr. Speaker, I would refer you to recommendation 108.
The committee recommends that the function of the subcommittee be to review the budgets of security and intelligence organizations with a view to providing reports to such committees as the House of Commons may determine and to review the work undertaken by SIRC and the Inspector General and to undertake reviews of a general nature -
That is a very positive recommendation and will go a long way, not only to protecting Canadians, but also to protecting the organizations that would be within the spectre of this review because they would have the benefit of parliamentary oversight.
It is shocking to look at the Estimates and see that this department has spent roughly $200 million over the last year and all we know is that it is a one-line item in the Estimates. That, quite frankly, is unacceptable. There must be more parliamentary involvement in that process. We should not allow $200 million to be spent and not have any idea where it went. Did it go for employees, for buildings, for equipment? What was it utilized for? Parliament has no idea at all.
In the United States, for instance, they have two oversight committees, one each in the House of Representatives and the Senate. They do check to see where the money is spent and whether they are getting a proper expenditure of funding rather than a cursory examination of funding.
We have heard it said time and time again that about 95 per cent of the information these agencies gather comes out of newspapers and 5 per cent is secret. If that is the case, I do not see where an oversight committee would be of that much harm to the organization.
Additionally, another important recommendation was to have SIRC actually review all of the agencies involved in security intelligence, not just CSIS. That was in Recommendation 87 and that becomes very essential.

February 26, 1991
However, parliamentary oversight is more critical because of what this government has done in the appointment process of SIRC. John Bassett's appointment, in effect, sullied the whole operation of SIRC. It is absolutely necessary that parliamentary oversight be provided, and provided so that Canadians have confidence in what is actually taking place.
We must remember we are dealing with human rights here, and we are dealing with intrusions into people's private lives. In those circumstances, we must be most vigilant. If you politicize the agency that is actually going to be checking on CSIS, by politicizing the appointment process, then you really are putting human rights in jeopardy. That is why parliamentary oversight must occur. That is why, I am sure, most members of the committee, including government members, were concerned that that recommendation was not picked up in the Solicitor General's response.
I think, too, that the whole committee system in Parliament is now under threat or on trial here. There is an obligation to respond to committees and to enact at least in part, what has been done by these hard-working committees. To be treated in this cursory way is unsatisfactory.
I know that my time is going by. In conclusion, I would like to say that maybe the justice committee should take the suggestion of the chairman of the committee and enact a parliamentary oversight committee in spite of the government. I hope that can be achieved.

Mr. Speaker, in 1986, the Conservatives caved in to pressures from the United States government and signed the Softwood Lumber Thrift Memorandum of Understanding.

Mr. Speaker, weekly newspapers are the backbone of the communications system of rural Canada. This is why, for years, the Government of Canada has supported through subsidization the distribution of what are called community newspapers.
Last year, the Department of Communications announced the withdrawal of a substantial amount of that subsidy. Unfortunately, this information failed to reach many weekly newspaper publishers who sold yearly
subscriptions last fall on the assumption that there would be no significant change in postal rates for 1991.

Mr. Speaker, once again the United States is considering oil exploration and development in the heart of the Arctic wildlife refuge in Alaska.
The Arctic wildlife refuge along with the coastal plain and Canada's North Yukon Park constitutes the greatest most productive intact arctic ecosystem in the world. Oil development in the area will definitely jeopardize that ecosystem, and for what? For about 200 days worth of oil supply.
The Arctic National Wildlife Refuge is a calving ground for over 180,000 caribou which provide the basis of the economy of aboriginal communities in Alaska and the Yukon. The herd is also the largest in the world and a unique and priceless resource to all Canadians and Americans.
In July 1987, Canada and the U.S. signed the international agreement for the conservation of the porcupine caribou herd. The agreement calls on both countries to conserve both the animal and its habitat.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has been an advocate for the preservation of these lands and I urge the government to continue its opposition to the development of these lands which could forever destroy a priceless heritage. I further urge the Prime Minister to notify President Bush that the United States could be in violation of the intent of this international accord if development proceeds.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
Iraqi troops are now withdrawing from Kuwait, and yet President Bush has decided to pursue the war and to reject every proposal to bring this war to an end. I think Canadians would like to see the Prime Minister stand up and give an opinion on behalf of Canada and not simply echo the U.S. position.
Today the Prime Minister made a statement that he would like to see the Security Council hold a meeting to discuss compliance of Iraq with the resolutions.
I would ask the Prime Minister, in addition to that, will the government also support a cease-fire which can be monitored by the United Nations and support that cease-fire immediately? By any standards the war is won. When is enough enough?
Mr. Speaker, enough is enough when an aggressor nation indicates once and for all that it is going to honour all of the resolutions of the UN Security Council.
Hear, hear.

Iraq's Ambassador to the United Nations was asked at 12.30 today whether or not Iraq intends to honour all 12 resolutions of the Security Council, and his answer was no. He said: "Some of these resolutions may be invalid. We have our own reservations. Some of them lend sort of themselves to different interpretations. So we really have to take it step by step."
All members of the coalition, from Denmark to Great Britain to the socialist Government of France, today said the position put forward by the Leader of the NDP is unacceptable.

I have a supplementary question for the Prime Minister. At least, Mr. Speaker, the NDP has its own position and not just one that it copied from George Bush.

Mr. Speaker, all witnesses say the Iraqi army is withdrawing en masse. My question is still directed to the Prime Minister.
Will the Canadian government support the ceasefire to allow the withdrawal of Iraqi troops under UN surveillance?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for the New Democratic Party stated that the NDP has its own specific position. And indeed it does. It is practically the only party in this country and the only socialist party in the world that is taking this position. In France, they were saying this morning that France was favourable to putting a stop to the hostilities, provided all Security Council resolutions were strictly observed. However, it did not want to run the risk of dilatory manoeuvres at a time when its soldiers were engaged in combat. France believes it is up to the Security Council to take note of any official statements by the Iraqi authorities, that they agree to act on all the UN's decisions. That is France's position, it is Canada's position, and it is the position of any civilized country.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister and I are in agreement with one thing, and that is that the New Democratic Party is the only party that has had the courage to stand up and say: "Try diplomacy, try other methods and use war as a last resort".
We know that much of Iraq's military force has been destroyed, that in fact the UN resolutions that authorized force to ensure that Iraq withdrew from Kuwait, which is what the last resolution says, is being done, we understand, by the retreat of Iraqi troops. U.S. pilots have told reporters that while Iraqi troops are fleeing from Kuwait, they are bombing them with cluster bombs on the highways north of Kuwait City. In the words of one pilot, "we hit the jackpot."
My question to the Prime Minister is: Are Canadian pilots involved in this bombing of the retreat of Iraqi forces?

Mr. Speaker, Canadian pilots and CF-18 aircraft are fully engaged in the prosecution of the effort to ensure that the President of Iraq conveys, unmistakably, his complete acceptance of the 12 United Nations resolutions to

the Security Council. At that time and at that time alone would a cease-fire be appropriate, and would the Government of Canada instruct its CF-18s to cease and desist from the kind of action in which they are engaged in prosecution of the defence of the United Nations.
My hon. friend began with a prefatory remark that the NDP is the only party to try diplomacy and to try other methods. But she did not complete the NDP policy. It is also the only party that says that when we have to fight to defend freedom or the United Nations, count the NDP out.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to pursue some questions with the Prime Minister on the same topic.
I think we all recognize that this is a very crucial time and that there is a hope that the fighting can be brought to an end.
It is my understanding that the Security Council is meeting this afternoon and will be inviting the Iraqi representative in New York to present the case that the Iraqi government has announced and to determine its judgment.
What I would like to know from the Prime Minister is: Has Canada, according to the statements just made, already rejected outright this announcement of withdrawal, or is Canada going to await the judgment of the United Nations Security Council as to whether it meets the conditions or not?
In other words, are we prepared to await whether the Security Council itself decides that the conditions are appropriate, or have we already made up our mind?

Mr. Speaker, the informal meeting of the Security Council has just broken up. Iraq did not report. Iraq has not reported or responded to the Security Council. What Iraq has done is issue a radio broadcast. That is not the way to settle this dispute, and Iraq knows this.
The way that this matter can be brought to an end is for Iraq to come to the Security Council and to present its clear acceptance, as the Prime Minister said today
Oral Questions
unequivocally and clearly, of the resolutions of the Security Council.
As it has been from the beginning, the way to end this war has been in the hands of Saddam Hussein.

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs to clarify a point.
Is it not true that an outside country such as Iraq, while it is a member of the United Nations and not a member of the Security Council, cannot attend informal meetings of the Security Council, but that in fact there have to be formal meetings to which they can be invited? Under the rules of the UN that is not possible when it is in informal proceedings.
Will Iraq be specifically invited to make its case in front of the United Nations? Does the government believe that in crucial matters such as this it should be the UN Security Council that makes the judgments as to whether the requirements of the UN resolutions are being met, or is that a decision that is simply being made by the coalition partners? Where is the decision being made, by the UN or by the coalition?

The point is not who will carry the message. The point is that there is no message. Saddam Hussein has not indicated that he is prepared to accept the will of the world as spelled out in the Security Council resolutions.
With regard to who decides, the Prime Minister of Canada has made abundantly clear on a number of occasions and again today that the decisions rest with the Security Council, with the United Nations, with no one else, but before the United Nations can decide on the response by Iraq, Iraq must respond positively, absolutely and unconditionally to all of the resolutions set forth by the United Nations.

-in consonance with the resolutions of the Security Council. Openings towards the cessation of the conflict have been clearly revealed during the past two days. It would be tragic in the extreme if
February 26, 1991

the opportunities that have been created were now being lost. I appeal most earnestly that this not be the case.
