speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Worthy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs) and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make just a few final remarks about C-91, the act to amend the Financial Administration Act and other acts in consequence thereof.
I think that not only people in this House but people across this country, business people and other citizens, recognize that any business that tried to function in today's environment with rules and procedures that were over 40 years old would find it impossible. It would be inefficient and would not be able to operate long. That is the situation, in effect, that the Government of Canada now finds itself in. Although it has been manoeuvring around it, the rules and procedures that it operates under are 40 years old. I think it is recognized on all sides of the House that those procedures must be updated.
Bill C-91, therefore, is largely technical in nature. It is intended to make the financial management processes more efficient and to modernize certain procedures. The ultimate objective is to bring financial administration in the federal government into the modem electronic world. By permitting the introduction of new efficiencies and the use of electronic technology, these amendments would assist departments to do more with less to the benefit of all Canadians.
More specifically, the bill will improve the management of the federal government's cash inflows and outflows, increase the efficiency with which government
February 26, 1991

programs and services are administered, streamline and modernize internal administrative processes, provide enhanced tools to facilitate the management of the public debt and provide more flexibility in the funding and delivery of services, thereby providing better service to the public.
For example, the amendments to section 17(4) and (5) contained in clause 5 will eliminate the current cumbersome process that is involved in settling with banks and other financial institutions for NSF cheques received by the government.
This amendment will also pave the way for streamlining the process of paying fees and commissions to agents who act on behalf of the government, thereby minimizing the paper burden imposed on them.
It has long been an accepted practice for agents in the private sector to withhold their fees and commissions from the funds collected. This applies whether one is selling a house, a ticket to a sports event or a concert, or even selling real estate. Even the provincial government permits retail outlets to withhold their administration fees from sales tax collected.
But not so for the federal government. The full amount collected must first be deposited in the Consolidated Revenue Fund and then a separate cheque issued for fees and commissions payable.
The changes contained in this bill are long overdue and essential to fostering an efficient and businesslike approach to day by day transactions.
The bill also includes amendments designed to streamline and modernize the payment process. The amendments to section 34 will provide greater flexibility to use modem principles of risk management when verifying invoices and other claims for payment, while those to sections 35 and 36 mean that the government would truly enter the electronic age and take full advantage of electronic payment techniques. This would be of particular benefit to the government suppliers since payment would actually be in their hands on the due date. It also has cash management implications for large contributions and other major financial assistance to industry. With electronic payments, large cash advances would be eliminated and funds held in the Consolidated Revenue
Government Orders
Fund until the last minute. This means savings for the people of Canada and the Government of Canada.
Other improvements in the financial management process are aimed at streamlining the approval process for tax remissions, reducing internal red tape and other impediments to collecting at least part of the millions of dollars worth of debts currently deemed uncollectable. Those are dollars owed to the government, to the people of this country, that this government must make sure to collect if at all possible.
The bill provides uniform and consistent authority to waive charges and forgive money owed to the government on humanitarian grounds and where circumstances otherwise warrant. This, in fact, would make our government more human.
It also clarifies the requirements for recording and settling debts owed at the end of a fiscal year thereby eliminating any unwarranted overhead costs.
It reduces the paper burden by eliminating reports that nearly duplicate information already provided to Parliament through the expanded information now provided in part 3 of the Estimates.
In summary, this bill is designed to bring financial management practices in the government into the modem age and to increase productivity. This it will do without sacrificing or diluting the fundamental principles of parliamentary control of our expenditures.
I would, however, be remiss if in concluding I did not mention that during debate in this Chamber, and also in committee, certain concerns were expressed over the wording of clause 6 on user fees. These concerns related principally to ensuring that users would not be called upon to pay more than their appropriate share of the cost and, more specifically, that no one class of users would be expected to bear the cost of services provided to other users.
In addition, assurance was sought that the rules of the game would not be changed in mid-stream and that new adjustment factors would not be introduced without amending the original order and without providing users an opportunity to make their views known.

Government Orders
The government has listened to these representations and it has made every effort to accommodate them. I am convinced that the bill, as now amended, meets the essence of these concerns.
I am now in a position to thank all hon. members who helped with the implementation of the bill to this stage. I would ask for speedy and positive support of the bill today.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in this debate, and it is a pleasure to do so this afternoon, on third reading of Bill C-91.1 have a number of problems with this bill, but generally speaking, I think the government is to be commended for introducing this bill to amend the Financial Administration Act. This is very important. I agree with the parliamentary secretary when he says that the purpose of this bill is to bring this government into the twenty-first century, which is excellent, and in that case, I am delighted to support this bill. Not, however, as far as section 16 of the bill is concerned. That is why I would like to make some brief comments, and I also want to discuss another matter that concerns section 30 of the bill.

Perhaps, if I continue in English, it would be easier for me as well as for hon. members.
Clause 6 of this bill represents a serious power grab on the part of the government. I think it is apparent to all that it is so, in spite of the protestations of the parliamentary secretary.
I want to thank him for his consideration of the amendments I proposed in the House. I recognize that the government has accepted the principle of one of them, with a minor modification in language. In respect of the other, I submit that there is still disagreement between us as to the effect of the amendment, and certainly the effect of clause 6 of the bill that has been presented.
In my submission the new clause 6 represents an attempt by the government to take to itself the power to impose charges in the nature of taxes on Canadians in exchange for the services they receive from their government. The normal procedure, as everyone knows, is for the government to introduce a bill to provide for certain
services for Canadians. Parliament normally votes the funds on an annual basis through the Estimates for those services to be provided.
What the government has now taken on itself to do is the power to charge Canadians for those services based on the costs of those services without recourse to Parliament This is a fundamental objection I have to this clause. This clause in its amended form has enhanced the power of the government in this regard, and that cannot be denied. If it did not have to be enhanced we would not have this amendment before us. I think the hon. parliamentary secretary knows that full well.
What we have here is a case where the government has decided that it does not have to come to Parliament any more-it does not want to come to Parliament any more-in order to increase in effect the tax burden on Canadians. Parliament would have voted the funds to pay for the services and presumably those funds will continue to be voted. The government, on the other hand, can charge a fee for the provision of the service and thereby recoup the costs of the provision of the service and use the money presumably voted by Parliament for other similar purposes, such as enhancing other departmental programs and facilities that come under the same vote as authorized by the House.
I think it is important that Canadians realize that this House is losing power because of the actions of the government in proposing this bill and assuming for itself certain additional powers.
In my submission this amounts to taxation without representation. It is a subject that led to the American revolution, as we all know. It is a subject that is veiy important in a parliamentary democracy, that the elected representatives of the people are the ones that determine who shall pay taxes and on what basis. In other words, all tax bills are required to be introduced here and all taxes can only be raised after a vote of this House, except in cases where we have delegated that authority to the government.
What is happening here is the delegation of authority that submit is beyond reasonable limits. It gives the government far too much authority, more than it had before.
Having said that and having expressed my objection to that-and I will come back to that theme later in my speech-I want to turn to the specific clause that the
February 26, 1991

government has changed. Perhaps the easiest way is to look at the amendment I had proposed.
The words of the amendment that I proposed yesterday, which my hon. colleague, the member for Willow-dale, was so pleased to move on my behalf, requested a change in the wording of the bill and read:
"the service or use of the facility to the user or classes of user who
benefit thereby."
I am quoting the words and I know they sound out of context, but the purpose of the amendment was to ensure that where the government decided to charge a fee for the provision of a service only persons who benefit from the service would be required to pay the fee.
The government has raised an objection to the words of my amendment on the basis that the use of the word benefit is too vague in law and that it could be construed to mean that someone who used the service but was refused the privilege sought by the service would thereby claim not to have benefited and would therefore not have to pay.
I can understand the argument. I know that it is there. I can understand that perhaps the use of the term in law would cause confusion, whereas it was clearly intended that persons who use the service pay whether or not they actually gain in the sense of improving their lot by reason of the use of the service. Charges for the use of the service is clearly what is intended, and I will concede that.
I want to make it clear today in this House as far as I can that the amendment that the government proposed to my amendment, which was ultimately accepted on division by the House yesterday, was intended to cover the situation and ensure that people who use the service pay for it. Whether the benefit actually accrues to the people as a result of their use of the service may not be the criterion. Indeed it is suggested that is not. The user of a service may be charged, but the question of benefit will only be considered in the sense of one having had use, so the charge is to be paid by users.
I hope that that construction of the words which the government amendment contains will be in fact applied in the courts. I realize as a lawyer that the courts are reluctant to look at parliamentary debate as authority for what was intended in an act of Parliament when the
Government Orders
words are in fact passed. However, if there is any reference in the courts to the use of this section, I hope that recourse will be had to my speech and to the parliamentary secretary's speech. Perhaps he wishes to clarify the point if I have misconstrued what he has said.
I would also refer, for the assistance of the courts, to the words uttered before the legislative committee that considered this bill. The person who was making the statements was the deputy comptroller general, Mr. McCrindell, on Tuesday, December 11, before the legislative committee on Bill C-91. In his statement he said the following as reported at page 1-15 of the transcript of the committee's proceedings:
When setting fees, program objectives and the effect on users and other directly affected parties are major considerations. The over-all objective will be to achieve greater equity in the financing of governmental activities by shifting the burden from taxpayers in general to those who benefit directly.
I stress the use of his words "benefit directly", which are not now in the bill because of the difficult construction of the word benefit in the English language. I hope when the matter comes before a court that the words used in the act will be construed very carefully to ensure that persons who do not benefit from the provision of a service-and I again use the word in its normal sense- are not charged for that service. Clearly that is not the intention of the government as stated by the deputy comptroller general in his statement to the legislative committee which we have attempted to put into this legislation by specific amendment.
There is one other item which I think has to be examined. We have not dealt with it in the House. I know we have now completed consideration of the amendments. They have been adopted in the bill. However, there is another item that was not included in the government's bill which is very important. Since this is an opportunity to amend the Financial Administration Act, I think it is one that we should look at in Parliament as something that should have been included in this bill. I refer to section 30 of the act which deals with the use of special Governor General's warrants.
I have dealt with this subject in Parliament before. I feel constrained to do it again today because the government has missed an opportunity to correct what I think is a serious flaw in our law. I do not think the flaw is actually in the law. I think it is in the government's

February 26, 1991
Government Orders
construction of the law and its use, or should I say abuse, of the system that is in place.
Perhaps I could review for hon. members for a moment the substance of our system of financial control which is, after all, the root of the powers of this House. It is a matter that led to the execution of a king in the United Kingdom. It is a matter that goes to the very root of parliamentary democracy. That fundamental principle is that there are no supplies or moneys granted to the government without the consent of this House. That is embodied in the legislation, in the Canadian Constitution. It is known that all Estimates must be voted first by the House of Commons. It is specified to be so in the Constitution of Canada. We know that supplies are voted by this House based on the Estimates which the government tables in this House. We are expecting a new set of Estimates on Thursday of this week, as I understand it, for the coming financial year.
In the 1988-1989 financial year and the 1989-90 financial year things were a bit different. Members will recall there was an election in November 1988, and the government saw fit to recall Parliament for two weeks in December. It discussed only one item of business, really, and that was the free trade deal. Rather than call Parliament back in the new year to vote supplies to complete the financial year, the government saw fit first of all to use a special Governor General's warrant pursuant to section 30 of the Financial Administration Act. That is exactly what they did on January 19, 1989. It got the Governor General to sign one of these special warrants authorizing the expenditure of $80 million from the public Treasury without a vote in Parliament.
Then on February 16, it did it again for $507 million without a vote in Parliament. The financial year, as we all know, comes to an end on March 31. In other words, it cleaned up the work of the old financial year but to avoid the difficulty of having to meet the House and get supplies voted, it then prorogued Parliament. Parliament was then in session but not actually sitting because it was adjourned. Rather than face any further difficulty, it prorogued Parliament and set a date for recall on April 3 or April 4, 1989. I have forgotten the exact date. That was into the new financial year. It had to have money to
operate for the first few months of the financial year and Parliament would not be able to vote money right away. That would take a few weeks. Instead of calling us back in March, as it should have done so that this could all have been dealt with, it waited until April 3 or April 4. On April 1, April Fool's Day, it went to the Governor General and got another warrant, this time for $6 billion. It was $6,175,011,778 to be precise.
It took that money and ran the government until Parliament got an interim supply bill passed in, I believe it was May 1989.
Shameful.

It was shameful. I am glad the hon. member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception recognizes that, because really what happened here was the first abuse ever of these special warrants.
It was the first time these special warrants had been used between sessions of Parliament, except for one isolated case in the early part of this century when there was some problem with the roof of this building.
I want to turn to section 30 of the act, and I want to stress the words of this section. It says:
Where a payment is urgently required for the public good when
Parliament is not in session -
When it is "urgently required for the public good". There was nothing urgent about these payments in this case. Parliament could have been recalled to deal with them. In every case these were payments for the general operation of the Government of Canada.
It was not a war situation where there was an emergency. It was not a case of government buildings falling down that needed immediate and urgent repair. It was not a case of a catastrophic event occurring in some part of Canada.
This was a case of a government unwilling to face the elected representatives of the people in this House. It was unwilling to come back and have us consider the question of the Supplementary Estimates or the Main Estimates. It simply said: "We will help ourselves by special warrant to this money." Never before had section 30 of the Financial Administration Act been so abused.
February 26, 1991

I have raised this issue in the House under questions of privilege. The Speaker has made rulings, and I recognize that we seem powerless to effect a change in that respect.
However, as MPs we do have some power to change the Financial Administration Act. I am disappointed that the government in introducing a substantial revision of this act as the parliamentary secretary has called it-and I agree with him that it is-would not have taken the opportunity to correct what is a glaring problem with the act if the government's interpretation of the act is accepted.
It has clearly been accepted for certain purposes, at least limited purposes, by the House because there is nothing else we can do as a minority in this House to object to this interpretation. However, I think it is an opportunity that the government might have taken up to make the amendment. I would have been glad to move it. But for the record I want it clear that such an amendment would have been out of order because it amended a section of the act that was untouched by the government's own bill.
I was instructed accordingly that the amendment would have been out of order had I attempted to move it. I have on the Order Paper a bill to amend the Financial Administration Act to prevent that kind of abuse, Bill C-211. I know I indicated my enthusiasm to the parliamentary secretary to ensure that that bill be incorporated as an amendment to Bill C-91, but apparently it was out of order and that could not be accomplished without unanimous consent. That was not forthcoming.
The difficulty is compounded in this case, in my submission, by one other little example of government arrogance. The government is required, under section 30, having used special Governor General's warrants, to make a report to the House. In accordance with the act, the government duly tabled a statement on special Governor General's warrants. In fact it tabled two: one for its use of the warrants in 1988-89 and one for its use of the warrants in 1989-90.
In the case of the 1989 financial year, that is the one ending March 31, 1989, there had already been laid before Parliament the Main Estimates which had been approved by the House, I believe in June 1988, although I was not here. Then there were some Supplementary Estimates tabled in the December session. Then another
Government Orders
set of Estimates, apparently Supplementary Estimates (C), were subsequently prepared but never tabled in Parliament.
They were referred to in the report that the government House leader, I believe it was at the time, tabled in respect of the use of the special government warrants. This happens to be Sessional Paper 342-1/258. The references in the opening summary where the portions of money not actually voted by the House are listed refer to a document as Supplementary Estimates (C), not tabled. Subsequent to the tabling of this document, one of the standing committees of this House conducted hearings in respect of the uses of these warrants. I may say that I had an opportunity at that committee to ask questions of the public servants who were responsible for the preparation of the special warrants and who obviously had something to do with the preparation of the supplementary estimates.
I asked at the committee hearing that copies of the Supplementary Estimates C referred to in the report be made available to members of Parliament. The witness before the committee on that occasion indicated that he would look into the matter and report.
Apparently he did report to the chairman of the committee and the reply that he sent to the chairman of the committee in June, 1989, which unfortunately did not get into my hands until I had sent some further correspondence on this in January of this year, indicated that, and I quote from the letter to Mr. Turner, the chairman of the consumer and corporate affairs committee: "I am advised that such a document, not having been tabled, constitutes a draft prepared only for the consideration of ministers and as such cannot be released".
That is where the matter was left. The document could not be released because, although it was Supplementary Estimates C, it was prepared in draft for tabling in Parliament had Parliament, in fact, been called to meet.
Although Supplementary Estimates C were referred to in the report we are not allowed to see them.
Why the secrecy? Why would the government seek to deny the production of these documents to Parliament? This is the body that is supposed to deal with the granting of moneys to the government for its purposes, yet it will

February 26, 1991
Government Orders
not make those purposes clear in this House by presenting this document.
Surely it was a reasonable request that those draft supplementary estimates be made available. Of course they were draft. Everybody knew that. But why is the government seeking to conceal those supplementary estimates from us in this House? I think it is a question that might be asked. We should have an answer.
I realize that, strictly speaking, this provision is not in the bill. It has not been dealt with in the bill, but it is an omission from the bill. It is an omission on the part of the government to table these documents. It is an omission on the part of the government to deal honestly and cleanly with this House in telling us what it wants the funds for because the purposes are contained in the estimates. That is where they are supposed to be and that should surely be made available to members of Parliament, even if we did not get a chance to vote on the provision of the money. That was taken away by the use, or misuse in this case, in my submission of Section 30 of the Financial Administration Act.
It is my submission that having looked at the abuse of this act, it is not surprising that we have had a change in attitude on the part of the public toward politicians and toward members of this House in general. I have here-

speechtext: I have a hundred letters on it.

Consistently over the last decade, Canadians have voiced an ominous degree of resentment against what they consider impersonal and inefficient intrusions by the state in their lives. respondents thought that politicians were competent, down from 57

If there is any place where the government ought to be making clear what it is doing, being honest and forthright in its management of public funds, it is in this House. It is in this place that we are charged with an onerous

responsibility of ensuring that the government is acting properly and of bringing the government to account if it fails to do so.
We, as members of the opposition, are crippled in our efforts to do that if full and complete financial information and estimates and so on are denied to the House.
Here we have a case where Supplementary Estimates (C), which were in draft have never made available. Here we have a case where the government, instead of calling Parliament and dealing with estimates in the usual way, chose to carry on in an unprecedented manner and help itself to the public treasury of Canada by special Governor General's warrants.
I have no trouble mentioning what I have said. The hon. member knows full well that what I have said is correct. He knows that the government did this in a way that was completely unprecedented. I suggest to him it was wrong and the government knew it was wrong. They chose to do it because they had no interest in facing the music that they would have to face in this House. They would have to face Question Period. They would have to face members making speeches on subjects that they did not want to hear about. So they sent Parliament away and said, "never mind, we will just take our money by special Governor General's warrants." The hon. member knows that is correct. He knows that what I am saying is true and if he looked at the record in a non-biased way, he would see that he would agree with me.
What we have here is a case of a floundering government that has failed to deliver on its promises and which has caused this loss of confidence, documented by Mr. Love in the article. I urge hon. members opposite to read it and, perhaps, they could appreciate the position that I have taken in respect to this bill.
To recapitulate then, I have three points. The bill is unfair in that it takes away from Parliament the right to impose taxes on the people. That is a fundamental right of this House and the government is taking additional powers from this House by this bill and in that respect, and particularly in respect of section 6, I believe that is wrong.
We have tried to get some safeguards in it. The amendments that the parliamentary secretary has proposed to mine in which I have improved the bill in my view may help. But we can only hope that they will be
Government Orders
construed in the way that it was intended they be when the bill, as it will undoubtedly be, is challenged in a court in Canada.
Second, the omission from the bill of the amendments to change the provisions aimed at special Governor General's warrants which would have stopped their use between sessions of Parliament in my view is a serious omission. Had the parliamentary secretary and his minister-who I am sorry is not here to hear my comments- got together and tackled this problem squarely, they would have realized that it would have restored some confidence in politicians, in this House and in its members.
Had they said: "We will in fact agree to such a restriction on our actions; we will come back to Parliament in future to get our money and stop dishing out the treasury to ourselves by the use of these warrants; we will come up with some amendment that will allow us to use them only in emergency situations, which was exactly the intention of the act", instead of acting as they have in violation of that act. I think we would have felt better about this bill, the public would have felt that perhaps things were not as bad as are shown in these polls, and we would have enhanced the reputation of the members of the House and the government.
I do not like to see the government always looking bad. I would prefer to see it look good and that is why we are here. It may look as though often times our criticisms are always negative, but they are intended to improve the government's performance.
The hon. member for St. John's East should be rejoicing in the fact that we try-
He is. Look at his smile.

I notice he is smiling-try to enhance the performance of his government because if it is not improved considerably, and I mean perhaps more than we could reasonably expect, his chances of re-election are so slight that I can only sympathize with his plight.
I say in conclusion, we have a bill here that could have been improved in two particular areas. I am sorry that the government has acceded in part to one but failed to act at all in the other. Accordingly, we will be voting against this particular legislation for those reasons,

February 26, 1991
Government Orders
although some of the initial clauses in the bill that deal with regular and normal administrative matters are sensible and wise. We feel that the omission and the one failure to correct the amendment that I had proposed, are insufficient to bring us to vote in favour of this particular legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak for a short while to this bill. I must say that Bill C-91 certainly took me by surprise when I was looking into the subtleties of how this would affect a number of things in my riding of Vancouver East, and in the country generally. I am sure that Canadians -and particularly Canadians in some of the industries that are directly affected and the workers that are directly affected-probably are not aware of the very negative and yet subtle changes that are being brought in in this bill.
I refer of course to the authority that is given under Bill C-91, an act to amend the Financial Administration Act of Canada. It gives authority to the cabinet to impose and increase user fees in a whole range of public services in Canada, services that the public has come to expect, and should expect, as their right and that should be paid for out of the general revenues by all of us who are taxpayers and should not be subject to user fees.
It is not surprising that this government is using this sneaky negative approach to get money out of people and they are imposing a marketplace approach so that people, regardless of their incomes, and corporations and businesses, regardless of their financial position, will be forced to pay user fees for services that they have rightfully expected to be public services and that should be available to them, regardless of income.
I think it is a very important principle of Canadian life and Canadian society. It is a principle that this Conservative government has continued to erode while they have been in power. It was bad enough under the Liberals, but it is becoming even worse under the present government.
Bill C-91 enables the federal cabinet to impose charges against users of government services without coming back to Parliament for parliamentary debate. They can do it in camera, in privacy of cabinet with no hearings or consultations with the people who would be
directly affected by these increased charges and, of course, with none of the committee process that we feel is very important when new measures are adopted. So in my view, it is a very dangerous bill. It gives the cabinet the chance to increase user fees which may seem to be token fees at this point in some cases, but I am sure will be increased under this budget and will continue to be increased with no public reference at all by the will of cabinet.
I would like to just take two or three examples. The more I thought about this and did a little bit of consultation into matters that I have a particular interest in and people on the west coast have a particular interest in, and I refer particularly to the Canadian shipping industry and also the shipbuilding industry.
I also would like to note that this reference to cabinet secrecy in imposing fees would mean that they could impose it on a whole range of social programs: health care, hospital care and certainly on rights of citizens. We already have user fees, for example, on applications for landed immigrant status, for passports, for taking out citizenship; things that have been the rights of Canadians and should still be the rights of Canadians. We should not be putting a monetary charge on them, they should be part of the services of Canada paid for out of general tax revenues.
I would like to concentrate first of all on the question of the shipbuilding industry. We know, of course, that the Canadian shipping industry is under attack from all sides, as is the shipbuilding industry itself. The government seems bent on destroying this industry.
I have been appalled, when I recall prior to the 1984 election, to when the Conservative platform said they were going to do so much to enhance and restore shipbuilding in Canada. They had what looked like a fairly good program that was part of their election platform at that time. They have gone on to do none of the things they promised and, in fact, step after step have eroded the industry, undermined it and removed the kind of essential subsidies necessary for any shipbuilding in a progressive and western country. I refer especially, of course, to the removal of all subsidies for shipbuilding that other countries know are essential if we are going to have a national shipbuilding program.

Second, of course, from a west coast point of view, the betrayal we felt and still feel because of the cancellation of the Polar 8. It is interesting to look back and see that the cost of the Polar 8 which would have been used to service our north in a peaceful way, to all of the community services in the north as well as act as an ice-breaker, was turned down. Yet, we have been able to find many more millions of dollars than that would have cost to conduct a war in the gulf. One wonders where our sense of values are in this.
I am told that the cancellation of the Polar 8 has already resulted in massive lay-offs of workers which could total up to 350 more workers, unless the government does something about this.
There has also been no assistance to the shipyards, which have been hit hard and many workers have been laid off. I know in the greater Vancouver shipyards have closed down as a result of this or they have had to curtail their operations and many workers have been laid off.
In the government policy on shipbuilding, and again I refer back to the negative impacts of Bill C-91. We have to remember also that the government has been really unfair in the allocation of contracts for the building, repair and refit of Canadian ships.
I would like to refer to a document I have here called: The Federal Government Response to the British Columbia Shipbuilding Action Group, dated February 1991.
The B.C. Shipbuilding Action Group proposed a number of amendments and stressed a number of problems. One of the things they documented was the unfair allocation of contracts that we have in Canada- the Coast Guard ships, the repair, refit and building of Coast Guard ships, icebreakers and naval vessels.
As you know, most of these contracts go to eastern and central Canada and it is, as is proposed in this brief to the government, essential that there be a fairer policy and that the shipbuilding needs, technology and facilities on the west coast be considered as well.
We know also, and this brief stresses it again, that there have been impacts from the free trade agreement on shipyards. This has certainly put B.C. shipyards at an unfair advantage. There is a need for a review of the tariffs on repair and maintenance of vessels. This bill, of
Government Orders
course, will add a further hardship and penalties to shipping and to shipbuilding industries. They already, of course, are charged user fees for Coast Guard services, for government wharfs, and for the use of many government services. The use of government facilities for cranes to move containers is another area.
Under this bill not only will the present user fees not be removed, but they will be increased quietly with no public notice and with no chance for the public to appeal them or even be heard as to their impact on an industry that already is suffering greatly and finding it difficult to compete with the American ports and the American shipping companies.
Bill C-91 means that the cabinet will make decisions in camera and that it will undoubtedly increase user fees for government facilities and equipment. There is particular concern about the effect on the competition of the port of Vancouver, for example, with the ports of Seattle and Tacoma.
It will also mean added costs for cruise ships in particular. There is a large trade related to cruise ships which stop in Vancouver, and a lot of spin-off business. The cruise ship companies have already complained about the heavy tariffs charged by the Canadian government which risk discouraging their use of Canadian ports. Increased user fees for facilities, which in turn will be passed along to the cruise ships, are enough to perhaps tip the scale and there is concern about the loss of this extra trade in the Vancouver region. I am sure the same thing applies to east coast ports as well.
I would like to take a minute to quote the concerns expressed by the Chamber of Shipping of B.C. regarding Bill C-91. The Chamber of Shipping of British Columbia has a membership of 50 locally based companies, the majority of international shipping companies that serve the B.C. coast and ports. They provide the link for efficient movement of western Canadian resources and goods to overseas markets and are essential to the entire economy of Canada.
The Chamber in a letter of January 28 to the Hon. Michael Wilson states that it has a great sense of urgency to draw attention to the proposed changes of the Financial Administration Act under Bill C-91, which enables the federal government to exercise the imposition of charges against users of government services

February 26, 1991
Government Orders
without parliamentary debate. It goes on to mention a number of ways the increase in user fees and proposed charges will affect domestic and international shipping under the cost recovery program. It anticipates that this is just the beginning of the escalation of these costs, which will have a very negative effect on the industry. The letter states, and I quote:
We fear that unchecked imposition of charges against shipping, could well pyramid to a degree that will strangle the ports on both coasts of Canada. Shipping and trade is a major part of the Canadian Gross National Product and diversion of cargoes by United States ports can become a real threat if costs continue to escalate.
Our industry now pays one hundred per cent of the Pilotage costs on the west coast, plus about one hundred and twenty per cent of the costs of running the Vancouver Port Corporation and the Prince Rupert Port Corporation, et cetera.
We feel strongly that authority to levy additional taxes against shipping by way of "User Fees" should be dealt with by Parliament and not by Cabinet without debate.
There you have it. Our party agrees very strongly with the position that the Chamber of Shipping of B.C. has taken. We are very concerned, not only with the present user fees that are being charged, but the authority that is given to cabinet to continue to add to these costs.
We implore the government to give consideration to this. It is not too late. We are at third reading of this bill, and we would like to see this bill delayed until it can be reconsidered.
In view of the philosophy of this bill, it is with great trepidation that we think of what is going to be in the budget today, or even what is not in the budget but what is going to happen despite the budget.
We may see that, for example, there are not drastic cuts in some of these areas, but drastic increases in user fees to increase revenue can be just as devastating to industries and to workers who are being laid off from essential industries.
There are many other areas that will be affected by the increase in user fees and the authority that is given to the cabinet to do this without any reference to Parliament.
For example, in my own critic area of multiculturalism and citizenship, particularly citizenship and immigration, it used to be that Canadian citizenship was regarded as a
right. That is, of course, what it should be. It should be a right in Canada.
We should not have to buy citizenship in Canada. We should not have to buy a passport. Surely, being able to obtain a passport is a right. Now, of course-this is just the beginning-we have to pay $25 for a passport.
If a person is applying for citizenship after they have been here three years, if a new immigrant is applying for citizenship he or she has to pay a user fee again to apply for this citizenship, instead of being welcomed by Canada.
What kind of a message does this give to new Canadians who have settled in our land? I spent the last month in my riding dealing with immigrant cases, the very desperate situations of many immigrants-particularly refugees-who have no medical coverage, no money to survive on and who are desperately afraid of their future and who are feeling very insecure.
When these people try to apply for landed immigrant status, even the beginning of the process, even though they may be turned down later, they have to find $250. Undoubtedly, that is going to go up under this bill.
You may laugh on the Conservative side about this, but I am telling you that there are people in my riding who want so much to be in Canada that they will be giving up food for their kids in order to try to find $250 which this government is charging for the right of residency in Canada.
I think that is appalling. It really defeats everything that we care about in Canada as far as the rights of citizenship are concerned.
I could go on and on, and I am sure my colleagues will, about what this means for the erosion of medicare. We already know what has been done to erode transfer payments to the provinces, both under the Canada Assistance Plan and the Canada Health Act.
This government is already eroding health care and basic social services in this country.
Now, we know that the cabinet can go ahead and approve user fees for services for hospitals and for other health care services. Is this the kind of Canada that we
February 26, 1991

want? The Health Care Act says that there is supposed to be accessibility and universal access to health care.
Yet, it is obvious that quietly-and we do not want it to be quiet, we are going to keep screaming about this-this government is undermining the whole principle of universality, equal access, accessibility, and transferability between provinces, because it is allowing provinces to charge user fees.
I will conclude at this point. I just want to say again that I think Canadians are unaware of the implications of this bill. It is a very dangerous erosion of the very principles of Canadian citizenship. The whole question of the cabinet having authority to charge user fees for essential public services, which our country has regarded as the rights of citizens that should be paid for by the income tax we all pay and tax revenues, is a disgrace. We are very much opposed to this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I understand that this bill is intended to help the government manage its finances more effectively and to help reduce the deficit.
In 1987, the federal government made similar proposals in Bill C-75. Today's policy proposal is very much the same, i.e. cost recovery in the marine and air transportation sectors. Mr. Speaker, instead of opting for additional charges, the federal government should consider implementing recent recommendations by the Auditor General of Canada, which suggested cutting costs and privatizing certain services to save money, instead of introducing additional charges.
Mr. Speaker, I also would like to point out that transportation should be considered within the global and intermodal context, instead of selecting specific sectors such as marine and air transportation. Railway and highway transportation are also very important.
Another aspect that should be considered is our national transportation policy as stated in Section 3 of the National Transportation Act. As I see it, the proposed fee schedule goes against certain elements of this policy. That is particularly true when we read that fares, rates and conditions set by each carrier or mode of
Government Orders
transportation shall not constitute an undue obstacle to the interchange of commodities between points in Canada. I must say the timing is very poor, now that shippers are being affected by the recession, soaring gas prices and the crisis in the Persian Gulf.
Mr. Speaker, they now want to charge overhead costs for the use of certain airports in remote areas in Quebec. This will hurt Abitibi and northern Quebec, where the price of a plane ticket will go up considerably.
Mr. Speaker, I received a letter from lawyer Jean Roberge with the Quebec mining association, who wrote the following to the Department of Transport: "In fact, cost recovery will mean increased costs for companies, which we will not be able to recover from customers who can find other suppliers on the international market. In Quebec, the expected cost increase would be at least 15 per cent on top of marine shipping costs of totalling at least 12 million. At this rate, Quebec companies will find it even harder to remain competitive.
The department explained that the cost recovery policy was developed in a spirit of fairness and efficiency. We disagree. We do not think it is fair to apply maximum distances of 300 nautical miles in Quebec, while other ports on our country's coasts are allowed a number well below those 300 nautical miles.
Mr. Roberge went on to say: "The proposed rates will cause considerable harm to the Canadian economy, especially in the primary sector. Canada and Quebec, which rank among the world's major suppliers of minerals and metals, may find their position will start to erode considerably". Those were comments made by Mr. Roberge of the Quebec mining association.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I would like to say that the federal Minister of Transport should consider the recommendations made by the Quebec mining association, the Quebec Minister of Transport and my own recommendations, to ensure that Quebec's and Canada's remote regions, as well as central regions like the Port of Quebec and the Port of Montreal, are not penalized by this bill.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Questions and comments. Resuming debate. The hon. member for Gander-Grand Falls.

February 26, 1991
Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, I will try to keep this very short. In fact, I should be able to finish my comment in about five minutes.
It is to present a matter of great concern to me, and to Canadians if they knew what was in the bill. The Financial Administration Act is used not only to levy fees and make charges in this bill, but also to introduce a new element into our legislation.
This new element affects all moneys owed to the Receiver General of Canada-and there is no other way under our legislation to write a cheque to the Government of Canada except to write it to the Receiver General of Canada. All of our legislation that has been passed in this Chamber ever since Confederation, every bit of it, contains regulations that spell out how money is to be recovered by the Government of Canada when it is due to the Government of Canada.
The bill that is being passed here today brings a new element into the picture. The new element is found in a new clause in this legislation called clause 17.1. It brings into play, for the first time in our history, the words "collection agency". The words "collection agency" are defined as a member of the legal profession or as a collector of debts registered within a province.
All of our legislation and regulations that contain provisions whereby somebody can pay back money over a period of time, and each part of our regulations, at least most of them, have a limitation on the collection of debts.
The Unemployment Insurance Act has a limitation of three years, unless it is fraud and then it is six years. The collection of debts relating to the Department of Finance or National Revenue, in the case of somebody who owes money to the Receiver General of Canada for the advanced child tax credit, should never be collected.
People owe that advance because they suffered a tragedy that caused their children to be absent from their homes in the month of Januaiy of this year. The legislation we passed in this Chamber in 1988 said that in order to qualify for the advanced child tax credit you had to be a resident in that home and receive family allowance for the following January. Some of the reasons for this absence, most of them disastrous, were fire in the
home, family break up, or a death in the home. Sometimes the children were in foster homes. Women, mostly, are now told this month that they have to pay back $2,000 or $3,000 to the Government of Canada.
In the regulations of the Family Allowance Act it is spelled out how that money is to be collected. It is collected by taking the GST credit or the federal tax credit or family allowances over a period of time. Some of these widows who experienced the disaster of fire or death in the home in the month of Januaiy owe $4,000 or $5,000.
Now all of those regulations go out the window. All of those Acts of Parliament go out the window. All of those accepted, humane methods of collecting money-and if you do not collect it then you do not get it-now go out the window with the introduction of the collection agency. This is the collection agency bill of the Government of Canada.
The only thing that I can surmise from this is that the Government of Canada is suggesting that perhaps the occupation of the future is going to be with collection agencies. It is a terrible change to our legislation. The Government of Canada should rethink it or not use it when this act is passed.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind our viewers that Bill C-91, of course, is a bill that deals with the administration of public moneys.

-the management of public funds and finances. [English]
I wanted to make three points and ask my colleague to react if he would, please.
Our colleague, the member of Parliament for Kingston and the Islands, indicated to the government that this was a good opportunity, if it chose to do so, to correct this special warrants concern he has raised a number of times in Parliament, that is where the government uses special warrants in order to use public funds without referring to Parliament. I am wondering whether or not he would choose, subsequent to my other questions, to comment on that.
February 26, 1991

The user fees issues is of course one of great concern to me because it is in a sense a camouflage tax. It is a hidden tax. It is an undeclared tax. Many of us will know that the government has introduced 33 tax increases since it came into power in 1984, including the goods and services tax, but no one has really looked at the number of undeclared taxes through user fees.
This is interesting, because if one looks at the public accounts one notes that the government was receiving in 1984 in revenue $70 billion per year. Now it exceeds $120 billion. There has been over a $50 billion increase in the "regular tax increases" of the 33 increases I have mentioned. How many other dollars are there in these hidden kinds of taxes? Is this not perhaps a less than on the table approach to taxation?
I have a number of concerns, being from western Canada, from Manitoba. I have heard colleagues in the House refer to the possible introduction of user fees in health and education, but they have also mentioned shipping and other modes of transportation such as airport and air transportation, transportation by trucks and other modes. They have also mentioned the possibility that user fees be introduced in agriculture, in mining, in communications and in forestry, and I will stop there.
What are the implications for western Canada-all Canada, obviously-where relatively speaking there is a fairly small population base and where the communities are dispersed, small, and frequently very far from each other. I would like to have a comment on that.
I would also like to complete my remarks by asking the following question.

I think it is clear the government should correct the deficiencies I just mentioned as, well as others identified by my colleagues, before proceeding with this bill.

Mr. Speaker, if I understand the hon. gentleman's question, that they will have to correct deficiencies that are presently in place before this bill can work, I have to agree completely with the hon.
Government Orders
gentleman and highlight the following example from this particular piece of legislation.
I refer specifically to section 29.1 in a new clause of this bill, which states:
A department may, in respect of its approved programs or authorized expenditures, be authorized by an appropriation Act-to expend revenues that it receives in a fiscal year through the conduct of its operations to offset expenditures that it incurs in the fiscal year;
The hon. members who are close to me from Moncton, New Brunswick, know that at this very moment air traffic controllers are holding negotiations with the Government of Canada to talk about wages. If this were correct, it would mean that air traffic controllers in Moncton, New Brunswick-the two members from New Brunswick next to me know exactly what I am about to say-and in Gander, Newfoundland and those air traffic control centres are making a profit for the Government of Canada. They charge air traffic control in this country, in case hon. members are not aware, for every initial contact made on a foreign carrier that goes across the Atlantic from Europe or from Africa or from the Soviet Union. Each initial contact costs that foreign carrier at least $150 per initial contact because of the service provided by air traffic control. But what happens to that money: $150 per initial contact? At about 500 contacts a day, that is about $25 million. Where does that money go?
A month?

That is about $25 million, give or take $4 or $5 million. Where does that money go? That money goes into the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
What we have in this bill, as the hon. member just pointed out, is a big fib. The money that goes into the Consolidated Revenue Fund of the Government of Canada is not credited to air traffic control, or we would not have the disputes in air traffic control in this country of not paying adequate compensation, of having to hire air traffic controllers from the United States to come up here, air traffic controllers who were laid off or fired eight years ago by the United States. We are not training enough in this country today, while they make millions and millions of dollars for the Consolidated Revenue Fund of the Government of Canada.

February 26, 1991
The Budget
This bill which says the department can use whatever revenues it generates in the expenditures within its department is not correct. I cannot use the word lie, so I had to say it is just a fib in the legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I realize it is very difficult for you to hear, given the volume of the background noise in the House today as we are awaiting the budget.
In the few minutes I have available, I realize that I will not be able to do more than just start my remarks. One of the reasons we are continuing to debate Bill C-91, when it was thought that it was going to pass very easily, that it was only housekeeping measures, is that it was discovered that there is a key clause in the legislation that would allow the government wide-open latitude to charge user fees, to impose new, almost tax regimes on the various components of the government operation.
One in particular is that of the Minister of Transport in terms of the marine industry. Many of us in this House are concerned about its long-term viability. In fact, we are concerned about the short-term viability of the maritime industry, whether it be on the west coast of B.C., the Great Lakes, the St. Lawrence River or the east coast.
This legislation if passed in its current form, particularly clause 6, will make it more difficult for a lot of our industry to survive. In doing so, it will also make it more expensive for many sectors of our economy-the grain sector, the iron ore sector, the coal sector, the potash sector, the forest industry, all of which must rely on at some point in time the shipment of their goods by ships whether it is domestically or internationally. This particular clause 6 will allow the government, through the Minister of Transport and his policies of cost recovery currently working their way through the system, to put the maritime industry in jeopardy.
We might ask why the government is doing so. Why is this particular clause include in this particular bill?
If I can go back to 1985 and another bill, the amendments to the Canada Shipping Act, the government at that time tried to include in the bill a specific cost recovery clause, clause 4. We successfully defeated that clause. We got the government to withdraw it. Through the back door it is now trying to do with this bill what it
failed to do with with Bill C-75. There seems to be some confusion in the government's own minds as to what is needed. In responding to the maritime ministry, the Minister of Transport and the President of Treasury Board say that they currently have the legislative authority to enact user pay.
In a letter dated December 17,1990 to the President of the Treasury Board, the Minister of Transport said the following: "It is my understanding that no new legislative authority is necessary to permit implementation of the department's proposals should it be decided in due course to do so. In the opinion of the Department of Justice, the existing section 19 of the FAA provides a sufficient legal foundation".
The question I must ask is: If they do not need it today, why did they feel they needed it back in 1985 under Bill C-75, the amendments to the Canada Shipping Act?
The government really needs this particular clause in order to have a solid legal basis for implementing the cost recovery measures currently being proposed by the Government of Canada through the Minister of Transport.
It is obvious to me from all the communications I have received from the industry and the communities involved that this particular bill is a serious threat to their economic viability. I indicated yesterday during the clause by clause debate at report stage that the clause should be withdrawn and that we would be quite prepared to proceed to receive third reading as long as that particular clause was deleted from the bill.
I do not know how much time I have left, but perhaps, Mr. Speaker, you might want to call it 4.30.
